--- title: "Looking before modelling" description: "Exploratory analysis as damage assessment, with the plots that find sentinel values, impossible depths and missingness that is not random." order: 3 categories: [eda, data-preparation] --- ## More than a polite preamble Exploratory analysis has a reputation as the polite preamble to the real work. Treat it that way and it will cost you a paper. A model will not tell you that your salinity column contains `-999`. It will fit happily, report a plausible score, and hand you coefficients built on a mean salinity of 2 PSU. Every problem in this section's dataset is visible in about ten minutes of looking, and invisible in the model output afterwards. The purpose of this pass is not to find results. It is to find out what is wrong. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. The R tab is what produced the tables and figures you see; the Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent, shown for translation rather than executed by the site. Figures stay in R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. It is real code, not pseudocode: it runs against the same files through `python/mlbasic_data.py`, and `python/check-snippets.py` executes every snippet in the site to keep it honest. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly**: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea A workable order, roughly cheapest first: 1. **Shape and types**: how many rows, how many columns, what did the reader decide each column was? 2. **Missingness**: how much, in which columns, and *is it patterned*? 3. **One variable at a time**: range, distribution, impossible values, spikes. 4. **Categories**: every level, with counts. Not a sample: every level. 5. **Two variables at a time**: relationships, and correlations you did not expect. 6. **The response**: its distribution, and the balance of classes if it is categorical. 7. **By group**: does anything differ by vessel, observer, year, gear? Step 7 is the one most often skipped, and the one that catches instrument drift. ## Worked example ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw <- load_coastal_survey_raw() dim(raw) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 815 17 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_raw raw = load_coastal_survey_raw() raw.shape ``` ::: ### Numeric ranges The highest-yield ten seconds in all of data preparation: print the minimum and maximum of every numeric column and read them as a scientist. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw |> summarise(across(where(is.numeric), list(min = \(x) min(x, na.rm = TRUE), mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), max = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE)))) |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", "stat"), names_sep = "_(?=[^_]+$)") |> pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = value) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|variable | min| mean| max| |:-----------------|-------:|-------:|-------:| |survey_year | 2018.00| 2020.49| 2023.00| |longitude | 140.01| 141.26| 142.50| |latitude | 41.00| 42.00| 43.00| |depth_m | 5.00| 102.68| 1581.00| |temperature_c | -999.00| -1.29| 16.03| |salinity_psu | -999.00| 2.24| 34.96| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 0.07| 1.42| 13.75| |abundance | 0.00| 3.88| 40.00| |catch_weight_kg | 0.00| 1.37| 13.26|
::: ::: ## Python ```python (raw.select_dtypes("number") .agg(["min", "mean", "max"]) # pandas skips missing values by default .T .round(2) .reset_index(names="variable")) ``` ::: Three things there should stop you. **Salinity has a minimum of $-999$ and a mean of 2.24.** No ocean is 2 PSU. This is the sentinel-value trap: some instrument or export wrote `-999` to mean "missing", and because it is a number, nothing complained. Temperature has it too. **Depth reaches 1581 m** on a shelf survey whose stations were meant to be under 200 m. **Chlorophyll has a minimum but the row count differs**: it contains real `NA`s, which is the honest way to record a missing value. ### Seeing the sentinel ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_sentinel <- ggplot(raw, aes(salinity_psu)) + geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + annotate("text", x = -999, y = 30, label = "−999\n(25 rows)", hjust = -0.15, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.5) + labs(x = "Salinity (PSU)", y = "Stations", title = "A number that is not a measurement") p_missing <- raw |> group_by(season) |> summarise(missing = 100 * mean(is.na(chlorophyll_mg_m3))) |> mutate(season = fct_reorder(season, missing)) |> ggplot(aes(missing, season)) + geom_col(fill = ml_palette[["orange"]], width = 0.62) + geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(missing), "%")), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.6) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) + labs(x = "Chlorophyll missing (%)", y = NULL, title = "Missing, but not at random") p_sentinel + p_missing ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Left: all salinity values. The real ocean is the sliver at the right; everything at −999 is a missing value wearing a number's clothes. Right: chlorophyll is missing far more often in winter: missingness with a pattern, which is the kind that biases results.](exploratory-analysis_files/figure-html/fig-damage-1.png){#fig-damage fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel is a histogram of salinity with a tall bar at minus 999 and a narrow cluster of real values near 34, separated by a wide empty gap. The right panel is a bar chart of the percentage of missing chlorophyll by season: about 1 percent in autumn, 2 in spring, 4 in summer and 19 in winter.' width=1700} ::: ::: That left-hand panel is the whole argument for plotting before modelling. One histogram, no statistics, and the problem is unmissable. ### Every category, with counts ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw |> count(substrate, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|substrate | n| |:---------|---:| |mud | 163| |Sand | 100| |gravel | 95| |SAND | 82| |Mud | 79| |muddy | 72| |sandy | 66| |sand | 57| |Gravel | 46| |Rock | 21| |rocky | 20| |rock | 14|
::: ::: ## Python ```python raw["substrate"].value_counts().reset_index() ``` ::: Four substrate types, twelve spellings. A model will treat `Sand`, `SAND`, `sand` and `sandy` as four unrelated categories, splitting the evidence for sand four ways. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The file actually holds fourteen Two of the original spellings had trailing spaces: `"mud "` and `"gravel "`. `readr` trims whitespace by default, so they were silently repaired before you saw them. That is convenient here and alarming in general: a different tool, or `trim_ws = FALSE`, gives you fourteen categories instead of twelve. Know what your reader is fixing for you. ::: ### The response ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw |> count(rare_species) |> mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|rare_species | n| percent| |:------------|---:|-------:| |no | 772| 94.7| |yes | 43| 5.3|
::: ::: ## Python ```python counts = raw["rare_species"].value_counts().reset_index() counts["percent"] = (100 * counts["count"] / counts["count"].sum()).round(1) counts ``` ::: The rare species is present at 5% of stations. Remember this number: any classifier you build for it must be compared against 95% accuracy, which you can get by answering "absent" every time. ### By group ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw |> filter(salinity_psu != -999) |> group_by(vessel) |> summarise(stations = n(), mean_salinity = round(mean(salinity_psu), 2), mean_temperature = round(mean(temperature_c[temperature_c != -999]), 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|vessel | stations| mean_salinity| mean_temperature| |:----------|--------:|-------------:|----------------:| |RV Kaiyo | 437| 33.75| 8.72| |RV Tsubasa | 353| 34.13| 8.41|
::: ::: ## Python ```python valid = raw.assign( temperature_c=raw["temperature_c"].where(raw["temperature_c"] != -999) ).query("salinity_psu != -999") (valid.groupby("vessel") .agg(stations=("salinity_psu", "size"), mean_salinity=("salinity_psu", "mean"), mean_temperature=("temperature_c", "mean")) .round(2) .reset_index()) ``` ::: The two vessels differ by 0.42 PSU in mean salinity, with no matching temperature difference. Two vessels sampling the same shelf should not disagree like that. This is an instrument calibration offset, and it would have been invisible in every plot that pooled the fleet. ## Six findings, six decisions Ten minutes of looking produced six findings, each of which is a *decision* rather than a repair: | Finding | The decision it forces | | --- | --- | | `-999` in salinity and temperature | Convert to `NA`, then decide what to do about missing values | | Depths up to 1581 m | Are these errors or real? Correct, drop, or flag | | Twelve spellings of four substrates | Standardise, and check no genuine distinction is being merged away | | Chlorophyll missing 19% in winter | Dropping those rows would delete most of winter | | Rare species at 5% | Accuracy is the wrong metric before you have even started | | One vessel reads 0.42 PSU high | Correct it, model it, or drop salinity entirely | None of these is answered by a tool. Each needs someone who knows how the data was collected, which is why exploratory analysis cannot be delegated to a package or an assistant. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Exploring can itself leak We have just looked at every row, and we will later hold some of them back as a test set. Strictly, anything you learn here, such as that salinity needs fixing or that winter is sparse, is information from the test set influencing your modelling choices. This is unavoidable and mostly benign; you cannot clean data you are not allowed to look at. Keep it benign by restricting this pass to *data quality* and keeping decisions about the response, and any choice made by comparing model performance, on the training data alone. [The leakage page](information-leakage.qmd) draws the line more carefully. ::: ## Limits of looking **Summary statistics hide what plots reveal.** A mean salinity of 33.9 after removing sentinels looks fine, and conceals that one vessel's values are systematically high. Plot by group. **Some errors are undetectable.** Of the twelve depths recorded ten times too deep, ten are obvious. Two of them, 125 m and 166 m, sit comfortably inside the plausible range and no amount of looking will find them. Cleaning reduces error; it does not eliminate it. **Automated profiling is a starting point, not an audit.** `skimr::skim()` and `naniar::vis_miss()` will show you the missingness and the ranges in one call, and neither will tell you that 1581 m is impossible *on this shelf*. That judgement is yours. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Exploratory analysis is damage assessment. Its output is a list of decisions, not a set of figures for the paper. - Print the range of every numeric column and read it as a scientist. Sentinel values and decimal errors surface immediately. - Count every level of every category. Twelve spellings of four substrates is normal, not exceptional. - Ask whether missingness is patterned. Missing-in-winter is a different problem from missing-at-random, and only the first one biases results. - Summarise by vessel, observer, year and gear. This is where instrument drift hides. - Some errors are simply undetectable. Cleaning improves data; it does not sterilise it. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Run `naniar::vis_miss(raw)` and `skimr::skim(raw)`. What do they surface faster than the code above, and what do they miss entirely? 2. Take the depth values above 250 m. Divide them by ten. Do the corrected values fit the depth–temperature relationship of the rest of the survey? That is the kind of evidence that turns a guess about an error into a defensible correction.
